_readme: FULL JOURNEY — exercises every field journey-runner.js actually reads, and supports all
seven --positive-control mutants. Reference example for skills/journey-proof.md;
field-by-field tour in skills/journey-examples.md; preconditions in fixture-seeding.md.
The domain is invented: a purchase-request app where an approver picks a supplier,
submits a request, and an approval record is written alongside it. Entities, widget
names, microflow names and BRD ids are all fictional. examples/brd/F101.brd.json is the
matching BRD fragment, so every requirement pointer below actually resolves.
Nothing in this file is asserted to pass against any real app. It is a SHAPE reference.
It has never been executed — see the honesty note at the bottom of journey-examples.md.
title: Purchase request — pick a supplier, submit for approval, land back on the list
_personaWarning: VERIFIED IN journey-runner.js: the runner never authenticates as `persona`. It logs in
via H.login(page) using cfg.user (env TEST_USER, default in config.js) and can fall back
to cfg.fallbackUser. On a fallback the runner records login INVALID and SKIPS every
journey, so the findings file contains one row and no walk. Keep TEST_USER and this
field in step, or the report attributes the walk to an identity that never made it.
_requirementNote: Journey-level pointers are the FALLBACK. A step that declares its own `requirement`
array replaces this list for every check that step records; a step that does not,
inherits it. Pointers are `<BRD id>#<JSON Pointer>` into analysis/**/F<NNN>.brd.json.
The runner treats them as opaque strings — it carries them into every finding and never
resolves or validates them. Nothing will tell you a pointer is dangling; that is why
examples/validate-journeys.js checks them against the BRD fragment when one is supplied.

seeds.name: supplierCode
seeds.sql: SELECT SupplierCode AS c FROM Procurement.Supplier WHERE Active = true LIMIT 1
_note: Every OQL column must be aliased — helpers.oqlScalar reads the first cell of the first
row, and mxcli rejects an unaliased SELECT. A seed that returns null or an empty
string aborts the journey as INVALID (instrument absent), never FAIL (feature broken).

seeds.name: supplierName
seeds.sql: SELECT Name AS n FROM Procurement.Supplier WHERE SupplierCode = '{{supplierCode}}' LIMIT 1
_note: CHAINED ON PURPOSE. Two independent `LIMIT 1` queries are not guaranteed to return the
same row, and then the journey types supplier A into the combobox and asserts about
supplier B. Seeds are resolved in array order and may reference any EARLIER seed.
`group` and `item` are the nav anchors' title attributes, clicked as a real user
would. Nav groups TOGGLE: clicking an already-expanded group collapses it, which
is why journeys must start from a reset state and never force-click nav.

_checksNote: BARE WIDGET NAMES here — the runner prepends `.mx-name-`. `ready` above is a FULL
selector. The two fields take different vocabularies; mixing them up produces a
selector like `.mx-name-.mx-name-btnNewRequest`, which is FAIL, not INVALID, and
reads in the report as a missing button.

actions.label: Supplier
_note: The combobox action asserts as it goes: it reads aria-activedescendant while
stepping the highlight, then re-reads the committed input value and requires it to
contain `match`. That produces a PASS row of its own ('combobox cbSupplier
committed the seeded value'). If no option matches, the action THROWS — the step
is FAIL and the journey stops. That is deliberate: a fallback to option 0 once
committed a valid neighbouring row and every downstream rung agreed with it.
`ordered` names are matched EXACTLY against the mx.microflow.name tag, so they are
module-qualified. `mustNotFire` names are compiled with `new RegExp(n)` and tested
against the same tag, so an unqualified name works as a substring match.
TRAP, VERIFIED IN THE RUNNER: the whole trace block — capture, guard, ordered,
assertNoErrors AND mustNotFire — runs only when `ordered` is present and non-empty.
A step declaring `mustNotFire` alone is silently never checked. Always pair them.
Declaring `ordered` also buys assertNoErrors for free, which walks ACTIVITY spans.
That is the only check that sees a caught error: the microflow span stays OK while
its CallRest activity is ERROR and the page renders normally.

_textNote: Both arrays are {{...}}-substituted, so they can assert about the SEEDED value and
not just about boilerplate. `textAbsent` is the rung that catches a screen telling
the user nothing was saved while the row is sitting in the database — five other
instruments call that state healthy, because by their own lights it is.
These are arrays of STRINGS. Do not drop a `_note` object inside them; the runner
will stringify it and assert the page contains it.

_note: assertSequence is a SUBSEQUENCE check over span start time: incidental microflows
between these two are tolerated, a reorder or a skip is not. Spans sharing a start
time are treated as concurrent and either order is accepted.

_deltaNote: Baseline is taken ONCE, before the walk starts, for every distinct `creates` entity
in the journey — not per step. After each step's check the baseline is advanced to
the observed count, so a second step creating the same entity measures its own
delta. `delta` defaults to 1 when omitted, so declare 0 explicitly if the step must

_note: TWO SEPARATE CLAIMS, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME CLAIM.
assocMustBeSet -> the FK is non-null. Measured as an assocGap: COUNT(*) minus
COUNT over an INNER JOIN, because the join silently drops
null-FK rows. It passes for a request linked to ANY supplier.
mustPointAt    -> the FK points at the SEEDED supplier. Without this, a run that
picked the wrong-but-valid neighbouring row is indistinguishable
from a correct one on every instrument in the harness.
SET-NESS IS NOT CORRECTNESS. Never present a green assocMustBeSet as evidence the
right row was chosen.
SCOPE CAVEAT, VERIFIED IN THE RUNNER AND WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS: both queries run
over the WHOLE table, not over the row this run created. assocMustBeSet therefore
goes red forever if one legacy row has a null FK, and mustPointAt goes green if
ANY row anywhere points at the seed — including one an earlier run wrote. It is
only a per-run claim on a fixture that is reset between runs. See fixture-seeding.md.
`entity` may differ from `data.creates` — this asserts about a SIDE EFFECT of the
step, the approval record written alongside the request. Omit `entity` and it
defaults to `data.creates`; omit both and the SQL is built with `undefined` in it,
which returns null and is recorded INVALID.

oql.label: an approval record exists for the seeded supplier's request
oql.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM Procurement.ApprovalRecord AS a INNER JOIN a/Procurement.ApprovalRecord_PurchaseRequest/Procurement.PurchaseRequest AS p INNER JOIN p/Procurement.PurchaseRequest_Supplier/Procurement.Supplier AS s WHERE s.SupplierCode = '{{supplierCode}}'
_note: A floor, not an exact count: the fixture carries history, so 'at least one linked
row now exists' is the honest claim. The +1 delta above is what proves THIS run
wrote one. A query with NEITHER `expect` nor `atLeast` is recorded INVALID, not
PASS — the runner refuses to print a green cell for a check that cannot go red.

outcome.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM Procurement.PurchaseRequest AS p INNER JOIN p/Procurement.PurchaseRequest_Supplier/Procurement.Supplier AS s WHERE s.SupplierCode = '{{supplierCode}}' AND p.Status = 'Submitted'
_note: RUNG 5, one query over the END STATE. Per-step deltas can each be right while the net
result is wrong: a request that saved, linked correctly, and then never left Draft
passes every rung above and fails here.
VERIFIED IN THE RUNNER: the outcome block is evaluated after the LAST step returns
normally. If any step fails its actions or its landing guard the runner returns early
and the outcome rung produces NO row at all — silence, not INVALID. Read a missing
outcome row as 'the walk did not get there', never as 'not applicable'.
